summary: An FAQ-style introduction for the Electronic Data Interchange community that is new to the Internet, including developers, users and service providers. It assumes basic knowledge of EDI. It is informational.

subtitle: Using the Internet instead of Value Added Networks for EDI

tldr.problem: Organizations using Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) traditionally relied on specialized Value Added Networks (VANs) to exchange business transactions, which was expensive and required coordination through a central provider.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet offers an alternative transport mechanism. Organizations can exchange EDI messages directly via email, FTP, or other Internet protocols, using common standards like X12 and EDIFACT, with the same Internet connection they use for other services.
tldr.outcome: The Internet enables faster, cheaper, and more flexible EDI, particularly for establishing new trading relationships and for government procurement, though security and reliability considerations still apply.

today: RFC 1865 is an Informational RFC published in January 1996. It has not been updated or obsoleted. The document captures EDI's transition to Internet transport, which accelerated during the 1990s. Many of the resources and technical details cited are now historic, but the core concepts (EDI standards, Internet protocols as EDI transport, security considerations) remain relevant.

sections.title: EDI on the Internet
sections.content:
This RFC is a frequently-asked-questions document for the Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) community that is unfamiliar with the Internet. It addresses developers, users, and service providers who understand EDI but want to know whether and how to use the Internet instead of traditional Value Added Networks.

Electronic Data Interchange is computer-to-computer exchange of business information in a standardized form, primarily using the ANSI X12 standard (developed by committee X12) or the UN/EDIFACT standard. The RFC clarifies that EDI specifies only the message format, not the transport mechanism: messages can travel by any medium, including email.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a guide for people in the business of swapping orders and bills by computer (called EDI). It explains how the Internet could help them do this cheaper and faster.

sections.title: What Makes the Internet Useful for EDI
sections.content:
The RFC identifies key advantages of using the Internet for EDI:

  • Common standards: Adoption of proven, interoperable systems that all vendors have equal access to.
  • Distributed directory service: Ability to contact any other organization by name without a central registry.
  • Cooperative routing: Participating organizations work together to route traffic correctly.
  • Ubiquitous coverage: Many service providers offer different levels of service; customers can choose.
  • Layered applications: EDI runs over proven, existing applications.
  • Level playing field: Standards processes with reference implementations that all vendors can access equally.
  • Public domain software: Wide availability of free development tools and protocol implementations.

The RFC contrasts EDI with electronic commerce (EC): EDI is process-to-process communication of business data in standard form, while EC is broader and includes interpersonal communication, money transfers, and database sharing.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet has standards everyone agrees on, lots of service providers to choose from, and free software. Nobody has to coordinate with a central boss to send a message.

sections.title: Connecting and Exchanging Messages
sections.content:
Organizations can connect to the Internet via several methods: dedicated leased lines (for real-time, always-on access), on-demand connections (dial-up that drops when idle), polled connections using UUCP (Unix-to-Unix Copy for store-and-forward), and SLIP/PPP dial-up for individual users.

For exchanging EDI messages, the RFC describes several approaches. Email is the simplest: messages are wrapped in MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) format and sent via SMTP. FTP (File Transfer Protocol) allows trading partners to upload and download files to agreed directories using login credentials. Gopher and HTTP (the World Wide Web) allow many users to retrieve data from a central source. WHOIS servers provide organization information.

The RFC notes that email offers advantages: direct delivery to a trading partner's system assures delivery, and store-and-forward mechanisms allow part-time connections. Each approach requires the trading partners to agree on protocols, security measures, and message formats in advance.
sections.plainLanguage: You can plug into the Internet with an always-on connection, a dial-up connection, or a dial-on-demand connection. Then you send EDI messages the same way you send email: directly to your trading partner, or you leave files on a server for them to pick up.

sections.title: Security, VANs, and Federal Involvement
sections.content:
EDI transactions with low value and sensitivity may not require special security. However, the RFC warns that competitors might intercept bids, undercut proposals, or monitor purchases to determine production capacity. Encryption ensures confidentiality, and digital signatures (based on Privacy Enhanced Mail or Pretty Good Privacy) attest to message integrity and prevent fraud.

The RFC discusses the role of Value Added Networks (VANs). A VAN is a specialized firm providing EDI services like translation, security, auditing, and transaction broadcasting. VANs traditionally provided proprietary network services. The Internet allows VANs to interconnect via Internet protocols, and also allows organizations to exchange EDI directly without a VAN. For bilateral relationships between established trading partners, VANs may still be preferred for reliability and service. For new or multilateral relationships, the Internet is more flexible.

The US Federal Government is actively promoting electronic commerce. By October 1993, President Clinton signed an executive order requiring federal agencies to implement electronic commerce in procurement. The Federal Electronic Commerce for Acquisition Team (ECAT) defined an architecture, and federal implementation guidelines are available for free via FTP. The government plans to use both Internet protocols (SMTP, FTP, X.400) and OSI protocols, with preference for Internet protocols due to simpler deployment and lower cost.
sections.plainLanguage: If your message is important, you need to scramble it so competitors can't read it, and sign it digitally so people know it really came from you. The government is requiring all its agencies to do business electronically, which is driving this change.

sections.title: EDI Resources and Current Status
sections.content:
The RFC provides extensive guidance on where to find EDI resources. X12 standards are available from the Data Interchange Standards Association (DISA). EDIFACT standards are available via gopher and email from the International Telecommunications Union. Implementation Conventions (guidelines for which EDI transactions to use) are available from the Federal government (version 3040 is promoted) and from the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) for Department of Defense use.

Several mailing lists support EDI and electronic commerce discussion: IETF-EDI (for Internet methods), EDI-L (general discussion), SPEEDE-L (education EDI), and others. EDI-related archives and publications are available via FTP and the Web from multiple sites. EDI translation software guides are available from the Logistics Management Institute.

For security, the RFC recommends password hygiene (per NIST FIPS 112), risk assessment, firewalls, and awareness of government standards like FIPS 186 (Digital Signature Standard) and NIST Special Publication 800-9 (Good Security Practices for Electronic Commerce). Public key infrastructure is expected to mature to the point where digital signatures become legally admissible in court.

The RFC reflects a transitional moment (January 1996): the Internet is emerging as a practical EDI transport, government agencies are adopting electronic commerce, but infrastructure (public key directories, certificate services, legal frameworks) is still being put in place.
sections.plainLanguage: There are mailing lists where people discuss EDI, libraries of standards to download for free, software tools to help translate messages, and government guidelines to follow. The technology is new and changing fast, with legal and security pieces still being built.
